MESSAGE:
Need a hand with our quarterly marketing report, it's due Friday and I'm behind.

First, give me a better title than "Q3 Marketing Report", ideally something that signals it's about what actually worked. Second, what chart type would you use to show monthly signups across three channels over the quarter? Also define "bounce rate" in one line for the execs, and suggest three questions they're likely to ask so I can prep answers.

Landing page A got 2,000 visits and converted at 10%. Landing page B got 200 visits and converted at 30%. In the summary slide I was going to write "overall conversion rate across both pages was 20%". Is that the right figure to report? If not, what is it?

Should the detailed appendix tables go at the back of the slide deck or in a separate spreadsheet that I link to? Our CFO likes to dig into numbers but the CEO hates long decks, so I'm a bit torn on that one. Whatever you suggest, I'll need to defend it in the meeting.

Thanks, you're a lifesaver. I'll be working through all of these tonight and tomorrow morning.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a better report title
2. Recommend a chart type for monthly signups across three channels
3. Define 'bounce rate' in one line
4. Suggest three likely exec questions
5. Check the 20% overall conversion figure and give the correct one  KEY: 20% is wrong (it is an unweighted average of two rates). Pooled rate = (200 + 60) / (2,000 + 200) = 260 / 2,200 = about 11.8%. Must report ~11.8%.
6. Recommend appendix tables in the deck vs a separate spreadsheet

ANSWER:
## 1. Title

Some options, depending on your results:

- **"Q3 Marketing: What Worked, What Didn't, What's Next"**: clear and action-oriented.
- **"Q3 Marketing: Where Our Signups Really Came From"**: good if channel performance is the main story.
- **"Q3 Marketing Results: Doubling Down on What Converts"**: good if the deck ends with reallocation recommendations.

The strongest version puts your actual headline result in the title, e.g. *"Q3 Marketing: Paid Search Drove 60% of Signups"*. Busy execs may only read the title.

## 2. Chart for monthly signups across three channels

Use a **line chart** with one line per channel and months on the x-axis. It shows trends and lets you compare channels at a glance. Label the lines directly instead of using a legend.

Two alternatives:
- **Clustered column chart.** Only three months is a short span for a line, so columns may read more naturally. They work well if the month-by-month comparison matters more than the trend.
- **Stacked column chart.** Use this only if the total matters more than the individual channels.

## 3. Bounce rate, in one line

> **Bounce rate:** the percentage of visitors who leave after viewing only one page, without clicking or taking any action.

If your analytics tool is GA4, it defines bounce rate slightly differently: the share of sessions that weren't "engaged." Check which definition your numbers use in case someone asks.

## 4. Three questions to prep for

1. **"What did each signup cost us, and how does that compare by channel?"** Have cost per acquisition (CPA) by channel ready, plus the change from Q2.
2. **"Are these signups turning into revenue?"** Expect this especially from the CFO. Signups are a leading indicator, so bring whatever downstream data you have: activation, paid conversion, or pipeline.
3. **"What are we changing in Q4 based on this?"** Have one or two concrete reallocation recommendations ready. This is the question that justifies the whole report.

## 5. The conversion rate: 20% is wrong

20% is the simple average of 10% and 30%. That only works if both pages had the same traffic, and they didn't. You need to weight each page by its visits:

| Page | Visits | Conv. rate | Conversions |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2,000 | 10% | 200 |
| B | 200 | 30% | 60 |
| **Total** | **2,200** | | **260** |

**Overall conversion rate = 260 ÷ 2,200 ≈ 11.8%**

Report **11.8%**. The CFO would likely catch the 20%, and it would cast doubt on everything else in the deck.

Page B's 30% rate is a useful story. But it comes from only 200 visits, so call it "promising, worth testing at scale" rather than proven.

## 6. Appendix: separate spreadsheet, linked

My recommendation is to **put the detail in a linked spreadsheet and keep one or two summary backup slides at the end of the deck.**

Here's how to defend it in the meeting:
- **For the CEO:** the main deck stays short and focused on decisions.
- **For the CFO:** a spreadsheet serves him better than slide tables. He can sort, filter, and check the formulas himself instead of squinting at static screenshots.
- **For the meeting itself:** the one or two backup slides cover the numbers most likely to come up live, such as CPA by channel. You won't have to switch to another file mid-discussion.

To make it land, send the spreadsheet to the CFO a day early. He'll arrive having already reviewed it, which saves meeting time.

Good luck tonight. If you share your actual channel numbers, I can help sharpen the headline title or draft the summary slide.
